title: Chapter 7 Drill: Reproductive Endocrinology, Infertility, Menopause, and Contraception

items.stem: A 5-year-old girl has vaginal bleeding, breast enlargement, a large pigmented skin patch with an irregular border, and a bone lesion on radiography. Luteinizing hormone is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: McCune-Albright syndrome
Central precocious puberty from a hypothalamic hamartoma
Classic salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Premature adrenarche
items.explanation: McCune-Albright syndrome combines peripheral precocious puberty from autonomous ovarian estrogen production with pigmented skin macules and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia. Gonadotropins are suppressed because estrogen arises outside the axis. A hamartoma would give a pubertal luteinizing hormone response and no bone or skin findings. Classic adrenal hyperplasia causes virilization in girls, and premature adrenarche gives pubic hair and odor without breast growth or bleeding.

items.stem: A 17-year-old with primary amenorrhea has a mosaic karyotype of 45,X with Y chromosome material. Pelvic ultrasonography shows streak gonads. What is the most appropriate recommendation regarding her gonads?
options: Annual tumor marker measurement with retained gonads
Observation because streak tissue is nonfunctional
Gonadectomy because of the risk of gonadoblastoma
Oral progestogen to suppress gonadal tissue
items.explanation: Y chromosome material in a patient with dysgenetic gonads carries a substantial risk of gonadoblastoma, so prophylactic gonadectomy is recommended. Tumor markers do not detect gonadoblastoma early and are not a substitute for removal. Streak tissue is not harmless merely because it makes no hormones, since malignant change arises in the gonad itself. A progestogen does nothing to the risk of neoplastic transformation.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with 2 years of infertility and chronic pelvic pain has minimal stage I endometriosis found at laparoscopy. Her partner has normal semen parameters. What management increases her spontaneous pregnancy rate modestly?
options: Long-term gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist therapy
Laparoscopic ablation or excision of the lesions
Oral contraceptive pills for 6 months
Progestin suppression until conception is desired
items.explanation: For minimal or mild endometriosis, ablation or excision of the visible lesions modestly raises spontaneous pregnancy rates. Medical suppression with agonists, pills, or progestins does not improve fertility and only delays conception, so it is not given for infertility alone. These agents may still help pain, but a patient who wishes to conceive should not be placed on contraceptive suppression.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has had no menses for 14 months and reports nightly hot flushes. She has no other medical problems. What is the best way to confirm menopause?
options: Clinical diagnosis based on age, amenorrhea, and symptoms
A repeat follicle-stimulating hormone level in 4 weeks
An anti-Mullerian hormone level
A pelvic ultrasonography for follicle count
items.explanation: Menopause is defined retrospectively as 12 months of amenorrhea after the final menstrual period, and in a woman over 45 with typical symptoms no laboratory test is needed. Follicle-stimulating hormone fluctuates in the transition and adds nothing here. Anti-Mullerian hormone and follicle count estimate reserve and are not used to diagnose menopause. Testing adds cost without altering the plan.

items.stem: A 21-year-old woman has menses every 3 months, facial hirsutism, and acne since age 15. Her body mass index is 24. Prolactin, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone are normal. Total testosterone is mildly elevated. Which statement about diagnosis is correct?
options: A polycystic ovarian appearance on ultrasonography is required
A normal body mass index excludes the diagnosis
She meets criteria with anovulation and hyperandrogenism alone
Insulin resistance on testing is required to confirm it
items.explanation: In adults, polycystic ovary syndrome is diagnosed when two of three Rotterdam features are present after mimics are excluded: oligo-ovulation or anovulation, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology. Anovulation plus clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism satisfies this without imaging. The syndrome occurs at every body size, and insulin resistance, though common, is not part of the diagnostic criteria.

items.stem: Four days after unprotected intercourse, a 24-year-old woman with a body mass index of 38 seeks emergency contraception. Which method is most effective?
options: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg
Ulipristal acetate 30 mg
A double dose of combined pills
A copper intrauterine device
items.explanation: The copper intrauterine device is the most effective emergency method, with a failure rate near 0.1 percent, and it can be placed within five days. Levonorgestrel works best within 72 hours and is less effective in women with obesity. Ulipristal is effective for 120 hours and better than levonorgestrel, but it is not as effective as the copper device. Combined pill regimens are less effective and cause more nausea.

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman with hirsutism started a combined oral contraceptive 7 months ago, with partial improvement. Her clinician adds spironolactone. What counseling is essential?
options: Potassium supplements should be taken daily to prevent hypokalemia
Reliable contraception is required because of fetal feminization
The drug works within one week
Pregnancy is safe if she stops it at conception
items.explanation: Spironolactone is an antiandrogen added after about six months of hormonal therapy when hirsutism persists. Because it can feminize a male fetus, effective contraception is mandatory. It raises, not lowers, potassium, so supplements are inappropriate. Hair changes take many months to appear, not a week. Stopping the drug only at conception exposes the embryo during the critical period of genital differentiation, so reliable contraception must be in place first.

items.stem: A 17-year-old girl is considering depot medroxyprogesterone acetate. Which counseling point about this method is accurate?
options: It lowers bone density during use, which recovers after stopping
It permanently lowers bone density
It is the most effective reversible method
It always causes regular monthly bleeding
items.explanation: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate lowers bone density during use, which largely recovers after discontinuation, and it can cause weight gain and irregular bleeding. Its typical-use failure rate is about 4 per 100, so it is less effective than the implant or intrauterine devices. Amenorrhea becomes more common with continued use, and the bone effect is not permanent.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman has a dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry result with a lumbar spine T score of negative 2.7. She has no fractures. Which statement is correct?
options: She has osteopenia and needs only observation
The diagnosis requires a fragility fracture
A T score below negative 3.5 is required
She meets the criterion for osteoporosis
items.explanation: Osteoporosis is diagnosed by a T score of negative 2.5 or lower, or by a fragility fracture regardless of score, so this value qualifies without a fracture. Osteopenia is a T score between negative 1 and negative 2.5. Requiring a fracture or a threshold of negative 3.5 would delay treatment of women at high risk. Management includes calcium, vitamin D, exercise, and a bisphosphonate.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with estrogen receptor positive breast cancer is about to start chemotherapy and wants future fertility. Which option is most appropriate?
options: Ovarian stimulation with gonadotropins alone and no other agent
Referral for oocyte or embryo cryopreservation using a letrozole protocol
Waiting until chemotherapy ends to consider any fertility treatment option
A gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist as the only measure
items.explanation: Oocyte or embryo cryopreservation after a short stimulation is the established preservation method, and adding letrozole keeps estradiol low in hormone-sensitive cancer. Stimulation can start in any phase of the cycle, so chemotherapy is delayed little. Gonadotropins without letrozole produce high estradiol. Waiting until after treatment risks irreversible ovarian damage, and a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist is only an adjunct and not a substitute.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman is diagnosed with premature ovarian insufficiency after two elevated follicle-stimulating hormone levels. She has hot flushes and no contraindications. What is the appropriate hormonal plan?
options: Hormone therapy for 2 years, then stop
No hormones, with calcium and vitamin D only
Hormone therapy continued until about age 51
Combined oral contraceptive pills until age 40
items.explanation: Women with premature ovarian insufficiency face long-term estrogen deficiency affecting bone, heart, and mood, so hormone therapy is continued until the average age of natural menopause, around 51. Stopping at 2 years or using supplements alone leaves bone unprotected. Contraceptive pills are not required, and stopping at 40 ends therapy about a decade early. Early treatment also protects mood and heart health.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman with 2 years of infertility has a cycle day 3 follicle-stimulating hormone of 17 mIU/mL and a low anti-Mullerian hormone. What does this result most reliably predict?
options: An inability to conceive spontaneously ever again
A poor response to ovarian stimulation
A high risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
An increased risk of tubal occlusion
items.explanation: Ovarian reserve tests estimate the quantity of oocytes and predict the response to gonadotropins, so these results suggest a diminished response and counsel earlier treatment with realistic expectations. They do not predict that spontaneous pregnancy is impossible. Hyperstimulation risk is highest with a high anti-Mullerian hormone and many follicles, the opposite of this picture. Reserve testing says nothing about tubal patency.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has had amenorrhea for 7 months with hot flushes. Her follicle-stimulating hormone is 82 mIU/mL on two samples taken 5 weeks apart, and the pregnancy test is negative. Along with fragile X premutation testing, which study is most appropriate?
options: Hysterosalpingography
Midluteal serum progesterone drawn one week before expected menses
Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone
Peripheral blood karyotype
items.explanation: Two elevated follicle-stimulating hormone values at least four weeks apart in a woman under 40 define primary ovarian insufficiency. A karyotype is advised under age 30 to find a Turner variant or Y chromosome material, which carries a gonadal tumor risk, and fragile X premutation and adrenal antibodies are also tested. Imaging of the tubes and progesterone timing address fertility, not the cause. A 17-hydroxyprogesterone level screens for nonclassic adrenal hyperplasia, which does not produce ovarian failure.

items.stem: A couple with 3 losses is found to have a balanced Robertsonian translocation in the husband. What is the most appropriate counseling?
options: Genetic counseling, with preimplantation or prenatal diagnosis offered
No future pregnancy can succeed without donor gametes or adoption instead
Treatment with aspirin alone will correct the risk
Cell-free fetal DNA can substitute for later diagnosis
items.explanation: A balanced translocation carrier is healthy but can produce unbalanced gametes, so the couple is counseled that an unbalanced conception is possible and offered preimplantation genetic testing or prenatal diagnosis. Many couples still have a healthy child naturally. Aspirin does not change chromosomal segregation, and cell-free DNA screening does not replace diagnostic testing in this setting.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman presents to the clinic with 4 months without menses. She has had unprotected intercourse, and her only complaint is mild morning nausea. What is the first test to order?
options: Serum follicle-stimulating hormone and estradiol
Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone and prolactin
Urine human chorionic gonadotropin
Pelvic ultrasonography for polycystic ovaries
items.explanation: Pregnancy is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhea and is excluded first in every patient who has had intercourse, before any hormone panel or imaging. The test is cheap, quick, and changes everything that follows. Follicle-stimulating hormone, thyroid function, and prolactin are the next tier once pregnancy is excluded, and ultrasonography for ovarian morphology has no role until a pregnancy and endocrine causes are considered.

items.stem: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman is 5 feet 3 inches tall, weighs 98 pounds, and her mother had a hip fracture. She has never had bone density testing. What is the best recommendation?
options: Wait until age 65 before screening
Vertebral radiographs every year
Serum calcium and vitamin D only
Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry now
items.explanation: Screening before age 65 is recommended for postmenopausal women whose fracture risk is raised by low body weight, prior fracture, glucocorticoid use, or a parental hip fracture. She has two risk factors, so absorptiometry is indicated now. Waiting seven years may miss early disease. Plain radiographs are insensitive to early bone loss, and laboratory values do not measure bone density.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman has vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, and recurrent urinary tract infections. She has no vasomotor symptoms and has an intact uterus. Lubricants have not helped. What is the best treatment?
options: Oral estrogen with a progestogen
Low-dose vaginal estrogen
Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis alone
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor
items.explanation: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause progresses without treatment, and low-dose vaginal estrogen is the most effective therapy with minimal systemic absorption, so a progestogen is not needed. Systemic therapy exposes her to unnecessary risk for a local problem. Antibiotics alone do not correct the atrophy that predisposes to infection. A serotonin reuptake inhibitor treats vasomotor symptoms, which she does not have.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman takes ulipristal acetate for emergency contraception. She wants to restart her pill the next day. What should she do?
options: Restart the pill the same evening without backup
Wait 24 hours and then use the pill as usual
Wait 5 days before starting a hormonal method, using a barrier meanwhile
Stop all contraception for one month
items.explanation: Ulipristal is a selective progesterone receptor modulator, so a hormonal method started soon afterward could reduce its efficacy. She should wait five days before beginning or resuming a hormonal method and use a barrier method in the interval. Restarting immediately or after one day does not allow enough time. Going a month without contraception leaves her exposed to a new pregnancy.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman taking risperidone has amenorrhea and galactorrhea. Prolactin is 62 ng/mL, thyroid-stimulating hormone is normal, and the pregnancy test is negative. What is the best next step?
options: Ask the prescriber about a prolactin-sparing antipsychotic
Start cabergoline immediately
Perform transsphenoidal surgery
Stop risperidone abruptly on her own
items.explanation: Dopamine antagonists such as risperidone commonly raise prolactin, so the first step is to coordinate with the prescriber about switching to a prolactin-sparing agent such as aripiprazole. Cabergoline may worsen psychosis by acting against the antipsychotic. Surgery is unwarranted with a clear drug cause. Abrupt discontinuation risks relapse of her psychiatric illness and should never be done unsupervised.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman with a history of hormone-sensitive breast cancer wants relief from hot flushes and is prescribed fezolinetant. What monitoring is required?
options: Serum potassium every month while she continues the drug
Liver enzyme measurement before and during treatment
Bone density every 6 months
Endometrial thickness every 3 months
items.explanation: Fezolinetant is a neurokinin-3 receptor antagonist that acts on thermoregulatory neurons without estrogen exposure, and it carries a warning for liver injury, so liver enzymes are checked at baseline and periodically afterward. Potassium is not affected, and bone density and endometrial thickness are issues for estrogen-related drugs, not this nonhormonal agent, which has no endometrial stimulation.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has had rapidly progressive hirsutism, voice deepening, and clitoromegaly over 6 months. Her total testosterone is 290 ng/dL. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start a combined oral contraceptive and reassess in 6 months
Order a cosyntropin stimulation test only
Pelvic ultrasonography and adrenal imaging
Begin metformin for insulin resistance
items.explanation: Rapid virilization with a testosterone level near 200 ng/dL or more suggests an androgen-secreting tumor, usually of the ovary such as a Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor, or of the adrenal gland. Imaging of both sites comes next, with dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate to localize the source. Contraceptives or metformin would delay diagnosis of a tumor. A cosyntropin test addresses nonclassic adrenal hyperplasia, which does not cause this tempo or magnitude.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman with a high anti-Mullerian hormone level and 30 developing follicles is at high risk for ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome during an antagonist in vitro fertilization cycle. Which strategy best lowers her risk?
options: Human chorionic gonadotropin trigger with immediate fresh embryo transfer and luteal support
Continuing gonadotropins for several more days
Adding oral clomiphene to the trigger
A gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist trigger with freezing of all embryos
items.explanation: In an antagonist protocol, triggering with a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist produces a short luteinizing hormone surge and a much lower risk of the syndrome, and freezing every embryo for later transfer avoids the pregnancy hormone that would prolong it. A human chorionic gonadotropin trigger with fresh transfer is the highest risk strategy. Continuing stimulation adds follicles, and clomiphene does not protect against hyperstimulation.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman has had two first-trimester losses with the same partner. She asks whether to wait for a third loss before testing. What is the best advice?
options: Evaluation is appropriate after two losses
Testing is advised only after three consecutive losses
Testing is advised only if a loss occurs after 12 weeks
No testing is useful at any number of losses
items.explanation: The American Society for Reproductive Medicine defines recurrent pregnancy loss as two or more losses, not necessarily consecutive, and encourages evaluation after the second loss. Waiting for a third or for a later gestational age delays identification of treatable causes such as antiphospholipid syndrome and uterine anomalies. Saying that testing is never useful is incorrect, since a few causes are both identifiable and treatable.

items.stem: A 15-year-old girl has short stature, a low posterior hairline, and no breast development. Her follicle-stimulating hormone level is markedly elevated and the karyotype is 45,X. Which test is most important to order next?
options: Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry of the lumbar spine
Serum cortisol after cosyntropin stimulation
Echocardiography or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging of the aorta
Fasting serum prolactin and thyroid-stimulating hormone
items.explanation: Turner syndrome is linked to bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, and aortic root dilation, so cardiac imaging is required at diagnosis and before any pregnancy. Bone density matters later and is addressed by estrogen replacement. Adrenal function is normal in this condition, and prolactin does not explain streak gonads with high gonadotropins. Thyroid function is checked over time, but the cardiac lesion carries the greatest immediate risk.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman is hospitalized with severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome. She has tense ascites, shortness of breath, and oliguria. Which intervention is most appropriate for her dyspnea?
options: Furosemide to promote diuresis
Paracentesis of the ascitic fluid
Immediate oophorectomy
Restriction of all oral fluids
items.explanation: Tense ascites compromises ventilation and renal perfusion, and paracentesis relieves both while the vascular leak resolves. Diuretics worsen intravascular depletion and hemoconcentration in a patient who is already volume contracted. Oophorectomy is not needed because the syndrome is self-limited. Oral fluids are encouraged, with intravenous fluids when needed, along with weight monitoring and prophylactic anticoagulation while hospitalized.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman and her partner have been unable to conceive for two years. Her evaluation is normal, and his semen analysis shows a total motile sperm count of 1 million. Which treatment offers the best chance of pregnancy?
options: In vitro fertilization with intracytoplasmic sperm injection
Intrauterine insemination with ovarian stimulation
Clomiphene citrate for the woman
Expectant management for another year
items.explanation: With severe male factor infertility and a very low total motile count, in vitro fertilization with intracytoplasmic sperm injection places a single sperm in each egg and gives the best chance. Insemination needs several million motile sperm to succeed. Clomiphene does not treat a male cause in an ovulatory woman. Waiting a further year wastes time without improving sperm parameters.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man had a vasectomy 6 weeks ago. His wife asks whether they can stop contraception. What should be done first?
options: Nothing, because the procedure works at once
A serum testosterone level
A scrotal ultrasonography
A semen analysis confirming azoospermia
items.explanation: Vasectomy is effective but not immediately, since sperm remain in the tract after the procedure, so a semen analysis to confirm azoospermia is required before unprotected intercourse. It does not work at once, and testosterone is unaffected because the testes continue to function. Ultrasonography does not show sperm presence. Neither vasectomy nor tubal sterilization protects against sexually transmitted infection.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman taking tamoxifen after breast cancer has severe hot flushes. She is already prescribed paroxetine by her primary care physician. What is the best change?
options: Continue paroxetine and add systemic estrogen
Stop tamoxifen to improve symptom control
Replace paroxetine with venlafaxine or gabapentin
Increase the paroxetine dose
items.explanation: Paroxetine and fluoxetine inhibit the enzyme that activates tamoxifen, which may lower its benefit, so venlafaxine or gabapentin is chosen instead. Systemic estrogen is contraindicated after breast cancer. Stopping tamoxifen sacrifices cancer protection to treat a symptom, and increasing the paroxetine would deepen the enzyme inhibition that the change is meant to avoid. Choose the drug that preserves the cancer therapy.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman with confirmed obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome and no prior thrombosis has a positive pregnancy test. What treatment should begin now?
options: Low-dose aspirin alone, started once the first ultrasound shows a heartbeat
Therapeutic-dose anticoagulation
Prednisone and intravenous immunoglobulin
Low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic-dose anticoagulation
items.explanation: Obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome without prior thrombosis is treated with low-dose aspirin and prophylactic-dose anticoagulation from confirmation of pregnancy, which improves live birth rates. Aspirin alone is not supported for this indication. Therapeutic dosing is reserved for women with prior thrombosis. Steroids and intravenous immunoglobulin lack evidence of benefit and carry risk, so they are not recommended.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman has headaches and bitemporal visual field loss. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a 14 mm pituitary mass, and prolactin is 480 ng/mL. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: Immediate transsphenoidal resection
Cabergoline
Radiation therapy of the sella
Bromocriptine at bedtime with no follow-up imaging
items.explanation: A prolactin-secreting macroadenoma threatens the optic chiasm, but a dopamine agonist shrinks the tumor and restores vision in most patients, so cabergoline is first-line even with visual symptoms. Surgery is held for resistant or intolerant cases. Radiation is slow and a late option. Bromocriptine also works but is less well tolerated, and follow-up imaging and visual fields are needed to confirm shrinkage.

items.stem: A 6-year-old girl is brought by her mother because of breast development and rapid growth over 4 months. Bone age is advanced. A stimulated luteinizing hormone level is in the pubertal range. Which treatment is indicated?
options: A gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist
An aromatase inhibitor for estrogen suppression
Medroxyprogesterone acetate given by injection
Observation with repeat examination in a year
items.explanation: Breast development before age 8 with a pubertal luteinizing hormone response is central precocious puberty, caused by early activation of the hypothalamic pulse generator. Continuous gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist therapy downregulates the pituitary and halts progression, preserving adult height. An aromatase inhibitor does not address the central axis. Progestins suppress menses poorly in this setting and do not stop bone maturation, and waiting allows epiphyseal closure.

items.stem: A 15-year-old girl began menstruating 2 years ago. Her cycles are irregular and she has moderate acne. Ultrasonography shows enlarged ovaries with many follicles. Her mother asks whether she has polycystic ovary syndrome. What is the best response?
options: The diagnosis is confirmed by the ultrasound findings
Ovarian appearance is unreliable this soon after menarche
Irregular cycles at this age always exclude the syndrome
A karyotype is needed to settle the diagnosis
items.explanation: During the first years after menarche, multifollicular ovaries and irregular cycles are normal, so ultrasonography or anti-Mullerian hormone should not be used to meet the morphology criterion within eight years of menarche. Diagnosis in adolescents rests on persistent irregular cycles plus hyperandrogenism, and a provisional label is often used. The ultrasound finding alone is not diagnostic, and a karyotype has no role in this presentation.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman with migraine with aura requests the contraceptive pill she used in college. She is a nonsmoker with normal blood pressure. What is the best advice?
options: Avoid estrogen and offer a progestin-only or copper method
The combined pill is safe because her blood pressure is normal
The combined pill is safe if she takes aspirin daily
Use the pill but at a lower estrogen dose
items.explanation: Migraine with aura is a category 4 condition for combined hormonal contraception because of the added stroke risk, regardless of blood pressure or smoking status. Progestin-only methods and the copper intrauterine device are safe alternatives. Aspirin or lowering the estrogen dose does not remove the risk. The estrogen component is the concern, so it should be avoided entirely.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman with polycystic ovaries receives gonadotropins and a human chorionic gonadotropin trigger. Five days later she has abdominal distension, ascites, hemoconcentration, and a rising hematocrit. Which mediator is chiefly responsible?
options: Prolactin released from the pituitary
Follicle-stimulating hormone itself
Vascular endothelial growth factor
Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary
items.explanation: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome follows human chorionic gonadotropin exposure, which drives luteinized follicles to release vascular endothelial growth factor, increasing capillary permeability and shifting fluid into the third space. Hemoconcentration and ascites follow. Prolactin and oxytocin are unrelated to this mechanism. Follicle-stimulating hormone induces the follicular growth but does not directly produce the permeability change. Vascular leak explains the fluid shift.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman smokes 20 cigarettes daily and wants contraception. She has no other medical conditions. Which method should be avoided?
options: The levonorgestrel intrauterine device
The copper intrauterine device
Progestin-only pills
Combined hormonal contraception
items.explanation: Smoking at age 35 or older, especially at 15 or more cigarettes daily, makes combined hormonal contraception an unacceptable risk because of arterial and venous events. Progestin-only methods and both intrauterine devices have no such restriction. Offering the levonorgestrel device, the copper device, or progestin pills is safe, and smoking cessation counseling should accompany any choice.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has 5 months of amenorrhea and bilateral milky nipple discharge. Her pregnancy test is negative, her thyroid-stimulating hormone is normal, and she takes no medications. Prolactin is 95 ng/mL on repeat testing. What is the next step?
options: Start clomiphene citrate to resume ovulation
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary
Order a karyotype and testing for fragile X
Perform hysteroscopy to look for adhesions
items.explanation: Persistent hyperprolactinemia after pregnancy, hypothyroidism, renal failure, and drug effects are excluded demands pituitary imaging to look for a prolactinoma. Treatment with a dopamine agonist follows if indicated. Clomiphene would not treat the cause and may be ineffective. Karyotype and fragile X testing evaluate ovarian insufficiency, which would have raised follicle-stimulating hormone, and hysteroscopy addresses scarring, which does not cause galactorrhea.

items.stem: A 32-year-old man has severe oligospermia with a total motile count too low for insemination. His partner is 31 with normal reserve and open tubes. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Intrauterine insemination with washed sperm after ovarian stimulation
Clomiphene citrate for the partner
Tubal surgery for the partner
In vitro fertilization with intracytoplasmic sperm injection
items.explanation: Severe male factor infertility is a principal indication for in vitro fertilization with intracytoplasmic sperm injection, which needs only a few viable sperm injected directly into each oocyte. Insemination depends on an adequate number of motile sperm reaching the tube and fails here. Clomiphene treats ovulatory dysfunction, which the partner does not have, and her tubes are already open, so tubal surgery is unnecessary.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman with polycystic ovary syndrome has 3 menses per year and does not want pregnancy. She declines daily medication. Which option best protects her endometrium?
options: A levonorgestrel intrauterine device
A daily folic acid supplement
A short course of clomiphene each cycle
Observation with an annual pelvic examination
items.explanation: Chronic anovulation leaves the endometrium exposed to unopposed estrogen, raising the risk of hyperplasia and cancer when fewer than about four bleeds occur each year. A progestogen is the protection, and a levonorgestrel intrauterine device delivers it without daily adherence. Folic acid has no endometrial effect. Clomiphene induces ovulation only for the cycle in which it is used, and a pelvic examination cannot detect early hyperplasia.

items.stem: A 9-year-old girl with a newly diagnosed leukemia requires immediate high-dose chemotherapy with gonadotoxic agents. Which fertility preservation option is available to her?
options: Oocyte cryopreservation after a stimulation cycle
Embryo cryopreservation with a partner
Ovarian tissue cryopreservation
No option exists before puberty
items.explanation: Ovarian tissue cryopreservation is the option for prepubertal girls, since stimulation of oocytes requires a mature hypothalamic axis, and for patients who cannot delay treatment. It is no longer considered experimental. Oocyte freezing requires pubertal development and stimulation. Embryo freezing needs a partner or donor sperm and a mature ovary. Saying that nothing is available would deny her a recognized standard option.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman delivered 3 weeks ago and is not breastfeeding. She requests the combined oral contraceptive pill. Why should it be deferred?
options: It lowers the supply of breast milk in all women
Thrombotic risk is highest in the first 21 days postpartum
It causes uterine atony in the puerperium
It raises the risk of postpartum depression
items.explanation: Combined hormonal contraception is category 4 in the first 21 days after delivery because the puerperium is already a hypercoagulable state and estrogen adds venous thromboembolic risk. Progestin-only methods and the copper device are safe alternatives. The concern about milk supply applies to breastfeeding women and is a secondary issue. Atony and mood effects are not the reason for deferral.

items.stem: A couple presents for infertility evaluation. The woman is 30 and has regular cycles. The man has never had a semen analysis. Which test should be ordered at the first visit?
options: Semen analysis
Hysterosalpingography
Diagnostic laparoscopy
Endometrial biopsy in the late luteal phase
items.explanation: Semen analysis is the simplest and least invasive test in the evaluation and is abnormal in a substantial share of infertile couples, so it is ordered at the first visit, before invasive testing of the woman. Hysterosalpingography and laparoscopy are more invasive and should not precede it. Late luteal endometrial biopsy to date the endometrium is no longer recommended for infertility evaluation.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with a prolactin-secreting microadenoma has conceived while taking cabergoline. She is now at 5 weeks of gestation with no headaches or visual changes. What is the best management of the medication?
options: Continue it at a higher dose throughout pregnancy
Switch to surgery in the second trimester
Order pituitary imaging every month
Stop it now and monitor symptoms during pregnancy
items.explanation: In most women with a microadenoma, the dopamine agonist is stopped once pregnancy is confirmed, because the risk of clinically important tumor growth is low. Symptoms such as severe headache or visual change prompt visual field testing and imaging. Continuing a higher dose is unnecessary. Surgery is not planned for a microadenoma without growth, and routine monthly imaging exposes the patient to needless testing.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman with polycystic ovary syndrome and a body mass index of 22 asks whether she needs any testing beyond her cycle management. Which screening is most appropriate?
options: Serum cancer antigen 125 every year for ovarian cancer screening
Endometrial biopsy every year regardless of bleeding
A glucose tolerance test or hemoglobin A1c, plus a lipid profile
Bone density scanning at the next visit
items.explanation: Insulin resistance occurs in polycystic ovary syndrome at every body size, so screening for impaired glucose tolerance and diabetes with a glucose tolerance test or hemoglobin A1c is advised, along with lipids, blood pressure, and sleep symptoms. Cancer antigen 125 is not a screening test for ovarian cancer in average-risk women. Biopsy is reserved for abnormal bleeding or risk factors, and bone density is not reduced in this syndrome.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman taking clomiphene citrate for ovulation induction reports blurred vision with flickering spots during treatment. What is the best next step?
options: Stop clomiphene and arrange an eye examination
Increase the dose to improve ovulation
Continue and reassure that this is common
Switch to a different cycle day for dosing
items.explanation: Visual symptoms such as blurring, scotomata, or flashes are an uncommon but recognized adverse effect of clomiphene, and the drug should be discontinued with an eye evaluation, since symptoms can occasionally persist. Raising the dose could worsen the effect. Reassurance and continuation ignore a reason for stopping, and changing the dosing day does not remove the drug exposure that causes the symptoms.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with a publicly funded insurance plan requests tubal sterilization scheduled in 10 days. She is 32 and has signed a consent form today. What is the problem?
options: She must be at least 40 years old
Consent must be signed at least 30 days before the procedure
Consent must be signed on the day of surgery
A spouse must co-sign the consent form
items.explanation: Federal rules for publicly funded sterilization require that consent be signed at least 30 days, and no more than 180 days, before the procedure, with a minimum age of 21. The patient already satisfies the age requirement. Consent on the day of surgery would violate the waiting period. A spouse signature is not required, and the counseling should cover permanence and regret.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has had her third first-trimester loss. Dilation and curettage tissue is sent for cytogenetic analysis, which shows trisomy 16. How should she be counseled?
options: A maternal thrombophilia is the likely cause
She requires parental karyotyping before a new pregnancy
The loss was likely due to chance, and the prognosis is good
She should receive progesterone in every cycle
items.explanation: An aneuploid embryo explains most sporadic early losses and points away from a maternal cause, sparing the couple a long search. The chance of a later successful pregnancy remains good, though risk rises modestly with age. Inherited thrombophilia is not a well-supported cause. Parental karyotype is reserved for specific indications, and progesterone has not been shown to benefit unexplained loss.

items.stem: A 16-year-old has never menstruated. She has Tanner stage 4 breasts, normal pubic hair, and a blind vaginal pouch. Pelvic ultrasonography shows no uterus. Karyotype is 46,XX. Which additional evaluation is most important before counseling is complete?
options: Serum testosterone to look for an ovarian tumor
Bone age radiograph to assess the pubertal growth spurt
Pituitary magnetic resonance imaging for a prolactin adenoma
Renal ultrasonography for associated urinary tract anomalies
items.explanation: Mullerian agenesis is frequently accompanied by renal anomalies such as unilateral agenesis or ectopia, and skeletal defects, so renal imaging belongs in the first evaluation. Ovarian function is normal, so testosterone is expected to be in the female range and tumor is not suspected. Bone age is for growth disorders. Prolactin excess would not explain an absent uterus, because her breast development and hair show intact hormones.

items.stem: A couple who each carry the cystic fibrosis gene mutation want a pregnancy without risk of an affected child. Which approach gives them the best chance of an unaffected pregnancy before conception?
options: In vitro fertilization with preimplantation genetic testing for the gene
Intrauterine insemination with clomiphene citrate and carrier counseling alone
Folic acid supplementation before conception
Amniocentesis at 10 weeks of gestation
items.explanation: Preimplantation genetic testing for a single-gene disorder analyzes embryos created by in vitro fertilization so that only unaffected embryos are transferred. Insemination with ovulation induction leaves the one in four risk unchanged. Folic acid lowers neural tube defects but not recessive disease. Amniocentesis is performed after conception and, at 10 weeks, is earlier than its usual window, so it cannot avoid an affected pregnancy.

items.stem: A 56-year-old woman has taken continuous combined estrogen and progestogen for 2 years. She now reports vaginal bleeding after 18 months of no bleeding. What is the next step?
options: Increase the estrogen dose
Reassure that late bleeding is expected on continuous therapy
Stop the progestogen and continue estrogen alone
Endometrial assessment by ultrasonography or biopsy
items.explanation: Bleeding after the first months on continuous combined therapy is not expected and must be evaluated for hyperplasia or cancer with transvaginal ultrasonography or endometrial biopsy. Raising the estrogen dose would stimulate the endometrium further. Reassurance risks missing a malignancy. Removing the progestogen leaves estrogen unopposed and increases the chance of hyperplasia in a woman with a uterus.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman taking an antipsychotic for schizophrenia has amenorrhea and galactorrhea. Prolactin is 70 ng/mL, and magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary is normal. What is the mechanism of her hyperprolactinemia?
options: Excess thyrotropin-releasing hormone stimulation
Autonomous prolactin secretion by a microadenoma
Blockade of dopamine receptors on pituitary lactotrophs
Reduced renal clearance of prolactin
items.explanation: Dopamine from the hypothalamus tonically inhibits prolactin release, so drugs that block dopamine receptors, such as antipsychotics and metoclopramide, raise prolactin. When the drug cannot be stopped, switching to an agent with less dopamine blockade is considered. Thyrotropin-releasing hormone excess occurs in hypothyroidism, which is not described. A normal magnetic resonance image argues against an adenoma, and renal failure is not part of the history.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman with a body mass index of 38 has bothersome hot flushes and no contraindications to hormone therapy. She has a uterus. Which route best limits her venous thromboembolic risk?
options: Oral conjugated estrogen with a progestogen
Transdermal estradiol with a progestogen
Oral estradiol at a higher dose
Intramuscular estrogen every month
items.explanation: Transdermal estradiol avoids first-pass hepatic metabolism and carries less venous thromboembolic risk than oral estrogen, making it preferable in women with obesity or modestly raised thrombotic risk. Her intact uterus still requires a progestogen. Oral preparations, whatever the dose, pass through the liver and increase clotting factor synthesis. Monthly injection gives unpredictable, high peak levels and is not a standard menopause regimen.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman had a hysterectomy with oophorectomy for benign disease 3 months ago. She has severe vasomotor symptoms and no contraindication to therapy. Which regimen is appropriate?
options: Estrogen alone
Estrogen plus a progestogen
A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor alone
Progestogen alone
items.explanation: After hysterectomy, there is no endometrium to protect, so estrogen alone is given and a progestogen adds only risk, since estrogen plus progestogen was associated with greater breast cancer risk in the Women's Health Initiative. A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor is an alternative for women who cannot take estrogen, not the first choice here. A progestogen alone is less effective for flushes.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman with infertility is scheduled for hysterosalpingography. When in her cycle should the procedure be performed?
options: During the midluteal phase, one week after ovulation
On the day of heaviest menstrual flow, to see the cavity best
In the follicular phase, after bleeding stops and before ovulation
Only after a negative serum progesterone
items.explanation: Hysterosalpingography is scheduled after menstrual bleeding ends and before ovulation, which avoids an early pregnancy exposure and a bleeding endometrium that can mimic filling defects. A luteal phase study risks irradiating a conceptus. Performing it during heavy flow obscures the cavity and increases discomfort. A progesterone measurement is not required, since the follicular timing already excludes a luteal pregnancy.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with epilepsy takes carbamazepine and uses combined oral contraceptive pills. She asks about a more reliable option. Which method is least affected by her medication?
options: Progestin-only pills
The levonorgestrel intrauterine device
The etonogestrel implant
The contraceptive patch
items.explanation: Enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs such as carbamazepine accelerate metabolism of steroid hormones and reduce the effectiveness of pills, the patch, ring, and the implant. Methods that do not rely on systemic hormone levels, namely the levonorgestrel and copper intrauterine devices and depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, are preferred. The implant and progestin pills lose efficacy with these drugs.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman has osteoporosis with no contraindications and no unusual fracture history. She has adequate calcium and vitamin D intake. Which is the usual first-line drug therapy?
options: Estrogen alone
Calcitonin nasal spray
Fluoride
A bisphosphonate
items.explanation: Bisphosphonates are first-line drug therapy for osteoporosis in most patients, reducing vertebral and hip fractures. Estrogen prevents bone loss but is not first-line for osteoporosis alone in women past the early postmenopausal years because of its risks. Calcitonin has modest effects and is rarely used. Fluoride produces dense but fragile bone and is not recommended.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with 2 losses has a normal examination. Which test is best for detecting a uterine septum, polyp, or adhesions as a cause of recurrent loss?
options: Serum anti-Mullerian hormone
Transabdominal ultrasonography in the midluteal phase
Saline infusion sonography or hysteroscopy
Endometrial biopsy to date the endometrium
items.explanation: Intracavitary and uterine anomalies are best demonstrated by saline infusion sonography, hysterosalpingography, or three-dimensional ultrasonography, with hysteroscopy for confirmation and treatment. Anti-Mullerian hormone measures ovarian reserve and does not detect a septum. A simple transabdominal scan misses subtle cavity defects. Endometrial dating has not been shown to predict loss and is not recommended. The test must show the cavity contour.

items.stem: A 13-year-old girl with Turner syndrome has no breast development and low estradiol. Her pediatric endocrinologist asks about starting puberty induction. Which regimen best mimics normal pubertal progression?
options: Low-dose estradiol with slow dose escalation, adding a progestogen later
A combined oral contraceptive pill started at a full dose now
Medroxyprogesterone acetate for 10 days each month from the outset
Growth hormone alone until breast buds appear spontaneously
items.explanation: Puberty is induced with low-dose estradiol, preferably transdermal, increased gradually over two or more years to promote breast growth, uterine size, and bone mass. A progestogen is added after breakthrough bleeding or when full dosing is reached, to protect the endometrium. Starting a contraceptive dose fuses the epiphyses early and blunts breast shaping. A progestogen alone cannot induce development without estrogen, and growth hormone does not substitute for estrogen.

items.stem: A 54-year-old woman, 3 years postmenopausal, has severe hot flushes disrupting sleep. She has an intact uterus, normal blood pressure, and a normal mammogram. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Systemic estrogen alone without any progestogen added
Systemic estrogen with a progestogen
Vaginal estrogen cream
Observation for another year
items.explanation: She is under 60 and within 10 years of menopause with no contraindication, so systemic hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms. Because her uterus is intact, a progestogen is required with the estrogen to prevent endometrial hyperplasia. Estrogen alone is appropriate only after hysterectomy. Vaginal estrogen treats genitourinary symptoms but does not relieve hot flushes.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has a 4 cm endometrioma, a low anti-Mullerian hormone, and 2 years of infertility. She is asymptomatic. What is the most efficient route to pregnancy?
options: Cystectomy followed by expectant management
Gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist for 6 months
Clomiphene citrate with timed intercourse
In vitro fertilization without prior cystectomy
items.explanation: Older women with endometriomas and diminished reserve do best with in vitro fertilization, since surgery on an endometrioma can reduce ovarian reserve further and she has little to spare. Expectant management after surgery wastes time. Suppression with an agonist delays conception. Clomiphene is aimed at ovulatory dysfunction, which is not her problem, and the chance of pregnancy at her age is low without assisted reproduction.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman presents 40 hours after unprotected intercourse and asks for levonorgestrel emergency contraception. Which statement is correct?
options: It will disrupt an established early pregnancy
A prescription is required for all women
A pregnancy test is not required before dispensing
It is effective only within 12 hours
items.explanation: Levonorgestrel emergency contraception prevents ovulation, does not disrupt an established pregnancy, and does not require a pregnancy test first. It is available without a prescription and is best used within 72 hours, with efficacy falling with delay. Advance provision is reasonable. The belief that it ends an implanted pregnancy is incorrect, and its window is far longer than 12 hours.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has had 3 losses, and a full evaluation shows normal antibodies, uterine anatomy, thyroid function, and parental karyotypes. She asks what can improve her chance of a live birth. Which response is most accurate?
options: Progesterone supplementation in every early pregnancy
Supportive care and reassurance, since most women still succeed
Intravenous immunoglobulin before each conception
Prophylactic anticoagulation from conception
items.explanation: In unexplained recurrent loss, the prognosis for a successful pregnancy is good without specific therapy, and early supportive care has measurable value. Progesterone and intravenous immunoglobulin lack proof of benefit for this group, and anticoagulation does not help women without antiphospholipid syndrome or prior thrombosis. Offering counseling alongside testing also reduces the emotional burden that couples carry.

items.stem: A 15-year-old with complete androgen insensitivity has been raised as a girl, and her breasts are developing well. Her parents ask when the intra-abdominal testes should be removed. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
options: Gonadectomy after puberty is complete
Immediate gonadectomy to prevent a malignancy
Lifelong surveillance with no surgery at any age
Gonadectomy before puberty to prevent virilization
items.explanation: In complete androgen insensitivity the tumor risk before adulthood is low, while testes provide the aromatizable testosterone that drives normal breast growth and pubertal bone accrual. Removal is therefore usually delayed until puberty is complete, followed by estrogen. Immediate surgery gives up that endogenous estrogen. Surveillance alone is not adequate because the risk of malignancy rises in adulthood. Virilization does not occur, since the receptor is nonfunctional.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman with polycystic ovary syndrome undergoes ovarian stimulation for in vitro fertilization. Five days after the hCG trigger she has abdominal distension, nausea, and weight gain. Ultrasonography shows enlarged ovaries and ascites. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Ovarian torsion
Ruptured corpus luteum cyst
Pelvic inflammatory disease
Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
items.explanation: Women with polycystic ovaries are at highest risk for ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, in which hCG exposure raises vascular permeability, producing enlarged ovaries, ascites, and hemoconcentration. Torsion causes sudden unilateral pain with a twisted pedicle. A ruptured cyst gives acute pain and hemoperitoneum without diffuse ascites. Pelvic inflammatory disease presents with fever and cervical motion tenderness.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman has persistent anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I antibodies and a prior deep venous thrombosis. She is now 6 weeks pregnant. What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan?
options: Prophylactic-dose anticoagulation only, as used for obstetric syndrome alone
Low-dose aspirin only
Therapeutic-dose anticoagulation with low-dose aspirin
No treatment until the second trimester
items.explanation: Antiphospholipid syndrome with a prior thrombotic event confers a high risk of recurrence in pregnancy, so therapeutic anticoagulation is given, usually with low-dose aspirin. Prophylactic dosing is for obstetric syndrome without thrombosis. Aspirin alone is inadequate protection against venous clot. Delaying treatment leaves her unprotected during the first trimester, when losses and thrombosis are both most threatening.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman has hirsutism and oligomenorrhea. Thyroid-stimulating hormone and prolactin are normal. Which test best excludes a condition that mimics polycystic ovary syndrome?
options: Midluteal serum progesterone drawn one week before expected menses
Serum anti-Mullerian hormone level
Fasting serum insulin
Early morning follicular-phase 17-hydroxyprogesterone
items.explanation: Nonclassic 21-hydroxylase deficiency presents in adolescence with hirsutism and irregular cycles and is screened for with a morning follicular-phase 17-hydroxyprogesterone, followed by cosyntropin stimulation if the value is borderline. Midluteal progesterone assesses ovulation, not a mimic. Anti-Mullerian hormone is typically high in the syndrome but cannot exclude another disorder, and fasting insulin is neither diagnostic nor required to exclude mimics.

items.stem: A 31-year-old euthyroid woman with recurrent pregnancy loss has elevated thyroid peroxidase antibodies and a normal thyroid-stimulating hormone. What is the appropriate management?
options: No routine levothyroxine for the antibodies alone
Start levothyroxine to prevent further loss
Begin prednisone for autoimmune thyroiditis
Order intravenous immunoglobulin before conception
items.explanation: Isolated thyroid peroxidase antibodies in a euthyroid woman do not justify routine levothyroxine for recurrent loss. Thyroid-stimulating hormone should be monitored, and overt or subclinical disease treated. Steroids and intravenous immunoglobulin lack proof of benefit and carry risks, so they are not given for unexplained loss. The evaluation should continue with the tests that change management.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman requests permanent contraception at the time of a planned cesarean birth. Which technique is preferred when feasible?
options: Bilateral tubal ligation with clips
Bilateral salpingectomy
Unilateral tubal ligation with fulguration
Hysterectomy for contraception
items.explanation: Bilateral salpingectomy is now preferred where feasible, because complete removal of the tubes lowers the later risk of ovarian cancer and eliminates the risk of ectopic pregnancy from a failed occlusion. Clips and fulguration leave tubal tissue in place and carry a risk of failure with ectopic pregnancy. Hysterectomy is not an appropriate contraceptive procedure for a healthy uterus.

items.stem: A 16-year-old nulliparous adolescent wants highly effective contraception that does not require daily attention. She has no medical problems. Which method is most appropriate to offer first?
options: Combined oral contraceptive pills
The contraceptive vaginal ring
Male condoms with spermicide
The etonogestrel implant
items.explanation: Long-acting reversible methods, such as the implant and intrauterine devices, have failure rates under 1 per 100 in the first year and are appropriate for adolescents and nulliparous women. Pills and the ring depend on adherence, with failure of about 7 per 100 with typical use. Condoms alone fail in about 13 per 100 with typical use, though they remain useful for infection protection.

items.stem: A 15-year-old girl has primary amenorrhea, short stature, and no breast development. Follicle-stimulating hormone is 62 mIU/mL. What is the best next step?
options: Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging
Cyclic progestin withdrawal
Peripheral blood karyotype
Growth hormone stimulation test
items.explanation: High gonadotropins with absent puberty and short stature point to gonadal dysgenesis, and Turner syndrome is the leading cause, confirmed by karyotype. Pelvic imaging does not define the cause. A progestin challenge is pointless because there is no estrogen to prime the endometrium. A growth hormone test addresses isolated short stature, not hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, and her elevated gonadotropins argue against any pituitary cause of growth failure.

items.stem: A 16-year-old girl has no breast development. She reports that she cannot smell perfume or food. Her follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone are both low, and the karyotype is 46,XX. What is the diagnosis?
options: Kallmann syndrome
Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
Turner syndrome with a mosaic karyotype
Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea
items.explanation: Anosmia with delayed puberty and low gonadotropins describes Kallmann syndrome, in which gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons fail to migrate with the olfactory placode. Constitutional delay is familial and has intact smell. Turner syndrome has high follicle-stimulating hormone from streak gonads. Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea occurs after energy deficiency in a girl who has already progressed through puberty. Treatment is sex steroid replacement, and gonadotropins later if she desires fertility.

items.stem: A 62-year-old healthy woman asks to begin estrogen to prevent heart disease and dementia. She is 12 years from menopause. What is the most accurate counseling?
options: Estrogen started now will reverse existing arterial disease
Hormone therapy is not recommended for prevention of those conditions
Estrogen is recommended for all women at age 60
Estrogen prevents dementia when started late
items.explanation: Current guidance does not recommend hormone therapy to prevent cardiovascular disease or dementia, and starting after age 60 or more than 10 years from menopause carries a less favorable risk profile. Estrogen does not reverse established atherosclerosis. It is not offered universally at 60, and late initiation has not been shown to prevent dementia and may carry risk.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman with 2 miscarriages has a positive lupus anticoagulant. What is the next step in confirming antiphospholipid syndrome?
options: Begin anticoagulation immediately without repeat testing
Order a thrombophilia panel for factor V Leiden
Repeat testing within 1 week
Repeat testing at least 12 weeks later
items.explanation: Antiphospholipid antibodies must persist to be diagnostic, so a positive result is repeated at least 12 weeks later because transient positives occur with infection and other conditions. Treating on one result risks unnecessary exposure. Inherited thrombophilia testing is not part of antiphospholipid confirmation. A repeat after one week is too soon to distinguish a transient antibody from a persistent one.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman has tried to conceive for 7 months without success. She has regular cycles and no known risk factors. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Begin the infertility evaluation now
Reassure her and wait until 12 months have passed
Proceed directly to in vitro fertilization
Order laparoscopy to look for endometriosis
items.explanation: Infertility is defined as failure to conceive after 6 months of regular unprotected intercourse in a woman 35 or older, so evaluation should start now, since age sharply lowers the chance of success with delay. The 12-month interval applies under age 35. Jumping to in vitro fertilization skips the basic diagnostic steps. Laparoscopy is invasive and reserved for suspected endometriosis or adhesions after less invasive testing.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has had 6 months of amenorrhea with hot flashes and vaginal dryness. Pregnancy test is negative, and follicle-stimulating hormone is 68 mIU/mL on two samples four weeks apart. What is the best next test?
options: Pituitary magnetic resonance imaging
Endometrial biopsy
Karyotype and FMR1 premutation testing
Clomiphene challenge test
items.explanation: Two elevated follicle-stimulating hormone values with hypoestrogenic symptoms before age 40 establish primary ovarian insufficiency. Evaluation of cause includes karyotype for X chromosome abnormalities and FMR1 testing for fragile X premutation, with adrenal antibodies as indicated. Pituitary imaging is for low gonadotropins. Endometrial biopsy addresses abnormal bleeding, and the clomiphene test assesses reserve rather than cause.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has had 2 first-trimester losses. Testing shows heterozygous factor V Leiden mutation. She has never had a venous clot. What is the best management?
options: Prophylactic anticoagulation throughout pregnancy
Reassurance, with no anticoagulation for this indication
Therapeutic anticoagulation from conception
Prednisone to suppress immune activity
items.explanation: Inherited thrombophilias are not well supported as a cause of early recurrent loss, and anticoagulation does not improve live birth in women without prior thrombosis or antiphospholipid antibodies. Routine thrombophilia testing is not recommended for this indication, so this result should not drive treatment. Prophylactic or therapeutic dosing exposes her to bleeding risk without proven benefit, and steroids have no role.
